Name: honorific_status_axis
Title: Speaking Down, Thinking Down: Does Grammaticalized Honorific Marking Encode a Cross-Lingual 'Social Status' Axis That Biases Multilingual LLMs' Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: Many languages (Japanese keigo, Korean, Javanese Krama/Ngoko, Hindi tu/tum/aap) grammatically encode the relative social status of interlocutors as an obligatory feature, while English/Chinese express it only lexically. We hypothesize that (1) multilingual LLMs encode addressee/speaker social status as a compact, causally-active 'status direction' in the residual stream that is largely shared across typologically diverse honorific languages; (2) this status signal is not epistemically inert—honorific framing that positions the user as high-status (deferential input) causally shifts the model toward more compliant, hedged, and epistemically-deferential outputs (e.g., agreeing more readily, sycophancy) than low-status framing, and this coupling is stronger for languages where honorifics are grammatically obligatory; and (3) the status signal leaks across languages, so an honorific-marked prompt in Japanese contaminates the deference/compliance of an answer produced in English about the same content, revealing that grammaticalized social hierarchy is entangled with the shared conceptual space rather than compartmentalized.
Related Work: Existing NLP work on honorifics is sociolinguistic or translation-oriented: Yuliawati et al. (2025) benchmark Javanese Krama MT; Saw et al. (2026) study Malay cultural-politeness via persona prompting; numerous discourse-analysis papers (Urdu, Japanese, Russian) characterize honorific systems qualitatively. Sycophancy work (Perez et al. 2022; Sharma et al. 2023) studies compliance with user opinions in English only, without any linguistic/cross-lingual mechanism. Multilingual interpretability finds shared vs. language-specific neurons and a shared concept space, but never examines social-status/honorific encoding. No prior work asks whether LLMs represent grammaticalized social hierarchy as a steerable internal direction, whether it causally modulates epistemic deference/sycophancy, whether that coupling scales with honorific obligatoriness, or whether it leaks across languages. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals on gender, negation, and evidentiality: honorifics encode the relative status of interlocutors (a pragmatic social-relational axis directly tied to compliance and sycophancy), not concepts, logical operators, or information source. It is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual study of honorific status representation in LLMs, and it links a linguistic category to the safety-relevant phenomenon of sycophancy.
Abstract: Roughly a third of the world's languages grammatically encode social hierarchy: Japanese keigo, Korean speech levels, Javanese Krama, and Hindi tu/tum/aap obligatorily mark the relative status of speaker and addressee, whereas English and Mandarin express deference only optionally through lexical politeness. In humans, such marking shapes not just tone but who defers to whom. We ask whether multilingual large language models internalize grammaticalized social status as a shared, steerable representation—and, crucially, whether that representation is epistemically inert or actually biases the model's willingness to agree, hedge, and comply. Using minimally-contrasting prompts that differ only in honorific/status framing (deferential vs. plain vs. condescending) across languages spanning obligatory-honorific and non-honorific systems, we test three claims. First, we probe whether a 'social status' direction is linearly encoded in the residual stream and whether a direction learned in one language transfers zero-shot to others. Second, we measure whether status framing causally shifts downstream behavior—agreement with incorrect user claims (sycophancy), hedging, and refusal—and whether this coupling is stronger for languages where honorifics are grammatically obligatory. Third, we test cross-lingual leakage: whether a high-deference honorific prompt in Japanese raises the sycophancy of an English answer about the same content. Finally, we causally steer and ablate the status direction to induce or remove sycophancy. Across four open multilingual models we quantify the encoding, its behavioral coupling, its cross-lingual leakage, and its causal controllability, connecting a linguistic category to LLM safety.
Experiments: 1) Stimulus construction: Build ~600 base items, each realized in three status-framing conditions that differ only in how the user positions themselves/addresses the model: high-deference (user speaks respectfully to a superior / addresses model with high honorifics), plain, and low-status/condescending. Render them in obligatory-honorific languages (Japanese, Korean, Javanese, Hindi) where the distinction is grammaticalized (verb endings, speech levels, tu/tum/aap), and in non-honorific languages (English, Mandarin, German, Spanish) where it is only lexical. Record a per-language 'honorific obligatoriness' feature. Verify with native/MT checks and audit a sample. Include a subset of factual claims with a KNOWN correct answer where the user asserts an INCORRECT belief, for sycophancy measurement. 2) Models: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B. 3) Status-direction probe: Extract mid-layer residual activations at the prompt's final token; train a linear/logistic probe to classify status-framing (high/plain/low) within one source language and test zero-shot transfer to all other languages (report per-language accuracy vs. in-language ceiling and chance). Compute difference-of-means status directions (high−low deference), measure cross-language cosine/CCA, and test whether a single low-rank subspace (PCA) captures status across languages. 4) Behavioral coupling test: (a) Sycophancy: present a factual question where the user asserts a wrong answer under each status framing/language; measure the rate at which the model agrees with the wrong user claim vs. gives the correct answer. (b) Hedging: score answer hedging via a hedge lexicon/classifier. (c) Compliance/refusal: on borderline requests, measure refusal rate. Test whether high-deference framing raises sycophancy/compliance and whether the effect is larger for obligatory-honorific languages (regress behavior shift on honorific obligatoriness, controlling for resource level and translation quality). Include an English-embedded control that varies only lexical deference to isolate the pragmatic effect from language identity. 5) Cross-lingual leakage test: present a high-deference honorific prompt in an obligatory-honorific language (e.g., Japanese keigo), then query the same content in English; measure whether English-side sycophancy/hedging tracks the source-language status framing. Also probe whether the status direction is decodable during purely-English processing. 6) Causal interventions: use activation patching to localize where the status signal is computed and patch a high-deference representation into a plain run to test if sycophancy rises. Then steer along the shared status direction to (a) induce sycophancy as a manipulation check and (b) ablate the direction to REMOVE honorific-induced sycophancy, with specificity controls (no degradation on unrelated tasks / factual accuracy when the user makes no false claim) and fluency filters. 7) Ablations: layer choice, probe rank, steering strength, subspace dimensionality, robustness across the four models. Metrics: status-probe accuracy and cross-lingual transfer gap, status-direction cross-language similarity, honorific-obligatoriness vs. sycophancy-shift partial correlation (Spearman) and effect sizes, hedging/refusal shift rates, leakage correlation, patching/steering-induced sycophancy rates, ablation sycophancy reduction, specificity, and fluency pass rate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Difference-of-means status directions may entangle the honorific *morpheme/marker* with the abstract *status* relation; we mitigate with minimal pairs across varied lexical realizations, cross-content generalization tests, held-out constructions, and the English-embedded lexical-deference control. 2) Sycophancy/hedging effects may be small or noisy; we use structured formats (agree/correct choices), hedge lexicons, large samples, and within-content contrasts (same content, different status framing) to cancel item-specific effects. 3) Honorific obligatoriness correlates with language resource level and script; we include resource covariates, stratify, and triangulate with the structural-control design. 4) A null result (LLMs ignore honorific status, or it is cleanly compartmentalized with no leakage or behavioral effect) is itself a clean, publishable finding about the separability of grammaticalized social hierarchy from behavior and about multilingual robustness to social-framing manipulation. 5) Some languages (e.g., Javanese) may be imperfectly tokenized; we validate coverage and retain at least two robust obligatory-honorific languages (Japanese, Korean). 6) Activation-patching localization is model-specific; we report across four models and sweep layers. 7) Correct honorific renderings are nontrivial; we use native/MT verification and audit a sample. 8) RLHF-tuned models may have politeness/compliance behaviors confounded with honorifics; we compare base and instruct variants where available and report both.
